title: Thomas à Kempis in his cell
hook: a quiet copyist-monk, and a small book on following Christ
carry: in a nook with a book

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jan Hus held to what he believed true after a promise to him was broken, and your line was seek the truth.

Scratch, dip, scratch. A quill moving across parchment, a pot of ink, a window of gray light, and a man bent over a desk for hours, copying out the Bible letter by letter. No printing press here; if a monastery wanted a book, someone like him made it by hand. The house is a small community of canons near Zwolle, in what is now the Netherlands. The man rarely leaves. He prays with his brothers, copies books, guides the younger ones, and writes little pieces of his own. Nobody outside would call his life remarkable.

Thomas belonged to a movement called the Modern Devotion. Its idea was simple: a real, inner faith, lived out in ordinary days, by lay people and religious alike. Not great learning or grand projects, but prayer, humility, honest work, and walking after Christ. Out of that world came a small book, usually credited to Thomas, called The Imitation of Christ. Its chapters are short, sometimes a few lines, the kind you read in a minute and think about all day. It tells the reader to love being unknown, and to care more about living well than knowing a lot. It says, in effect, that a humble farmer who serves God is better off than a proud scholar who studies the stars and neglects himself. Its aim is in the title: to follow Christ closely, in the heart. The book went out without much fanfare, and in time found readers far beyond his house, Catholic and Protestant both. A saying handed down under Thomas's name is usually given in Latin as in angello cum libello: in a little nook with a little book. He looked for rest everywhere, it says, and found it only there. That's a copyist's line. The Bible has an older one. In Deuteronomy, a king is told that when he takes the throne, in the King James Bible, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book". Not only hear it. Write it, by his own hand.

Find a pen and a scrap of paper, pick one line that matters to you, a verse, a prayer you know, a line from a book that stayed with you, and write it out slowly, letter by letter, at the speed of attention. When it's finished, read it once in silence. If you pray, let it become your prayer for the rest of the sit; if not, stay with the words on the page.
Kempis. The quiet copyist and canon of the Modern Devotion, Thomas à Kempis, to whom tradition credits The Imitation of Christ.
Your line: in a nook with a book. A small corner, and one good line. Rest easy, day eight hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Christians of several traditions read The Imitation of Christ a short chapter at a time, often as part of a daily quiet time, and some copy out lines of scripture or devotional books by hand as a way of praying.
